strengths: Substantial and valuable resource contribution to the fully open MLLM community: a 15M-sample SFT dataset with dual-level (short/long) CoT enrichment, a transparent curation pipeline (HoneyPipe/DataStudio) with released prompts, training recipes, and model weights — going beyond static dataset releases.

Well-designed ablation study that cleanly disentangles the effects of noise filtering (D_raw vs D_no-CoT) and CoT enrichment (D_no-CoT vs D_curated), plus a separate 1M-subset ablation comparing curated vs. random selection against the Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline.

Comprehensive evaluation across ~30 benchmarks spanning General VQA, chart/document/OCR, and math/reasoning; strong results on reasoning-heavy tasks (CharXiv-RQ, MathVerse, LogicVista) that directly support the CoT-enrichment thesis.
Detailed appendix documentation (per-stage training configs, filtering/verification prompts, noise case studies, qualitative examples) that supports reproducibility and transparency.

The dual-level CoT strategy is a sensible design: routing failed short-CoT verifications to long-CoT generation avoids discarding hard samples and inherently targets reasoning depth to instruction complexity.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: data cleaning, LLM-based filtering, LLM-as-a-judge verification, and CoT rewriting are all well-established techniques (e.g., MAmmoth-VL, LLaVA-OneVision); the paper's contribution is primarily an engineering/systematization of known recipes.

Internal tension in the 'fully open' narrative: the long CoT enrichment leverages undisclosed 'top proprietary MLLMs,' which weakens reproducibility of the pipeline and means the flagship 2.7M long-CoT portion could not be regenerated by the community. Also, verification against original responses risks propagating errors present in the original labels, with no human audit of data quality or reported filter/judge precision-recall statistics.

Comparability of benchmark results is a concern: the authors modified VLMEvalKit (extended LLM-based judging to benchmarks like DocVQA/ChartQA and patched MathVerse judging), and evaluate Bee-8B in thinking mode with 16K tokens. It is unclear whether baseline scores were obtained under identical conditions, which could inflate relative gains.

The 'new SOTA among fully open MLLMs' claim is selective: Bee-8B underperforms several baselines on DocVQA (87.2 vs 95.5), OCRBench, POPE, HallusionBench, and MMMU (66.8 vs Keye-VL 71.4); only a subset of benchmarks is highlighted in the main text.

No controlled experiment isolating the data contribution at the full 15M scale against a same-architecture model trained on an existing dataset (e.g., MAmmoth-VL or LLaVA-OneVision data); the core ablation is only at ~1M scale, and part of the gains may stem from the strong Qwen3-8B backbone and the GRPO stage rather than the dataset itself.

DataStudio/HoneyPipe, a stated central contribution, receives no quantitative evaluation of its own (e.g., cost, throughput, adaptability demonstrations); it is described only qualitatively. Minor presentation issues (cluttered Fig. 3, some typos) slightly reduce polish.

strengths: Substantial community resource: a 15M-sample SFT dataset, an openly documented curation pipeline (HoneyPipe/DataStudio), full training recipes, and model weights, which is valuable for the fully open MLLM ecosystem.

The ablation design is thoughtful: separating D_raw vs D_no-CoT vs D_curated isolates the contribution of noise filtering from that of CoT enrichment, and the Honey-Data-1M vs Random-1M experiment supports the value of the data selection strategy.

Broad benchmark coverage (30+ benchmarks across general VQA, chart/document/OCR, and math reasoning) and detailed appendices with prompts, training stage configurations, and per-stage ablations improve transparency.
The dual-level (short/long) CoT enrichment with fidelity verification is a reasonable and clearly described mechanism for tailoring reasoning depth to instruction complexity.
weaknesses: Potential benchmark contamination is not addressed. The training corpus aggregates dozens of source datasets that overlap with the evaluation benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA, DocVQA, OCR-VQA, ScienceQA, MathV360K, A-OKVQA, GQA, TabMWP, ArxivQA, GeoQA+, etc.), some of which are themselves derived from benchmark test sets, yet no decontamination analysis or discussion is provided. Given the paper's headline claim of SOTA on CharXiv, DocVQA, and math benchmarks, this omission seriously undermines the validity of the central claims.

The 'fully open' framing is misleading. The long CoT data is generated by 'top proprietary MLLMs' (unnamed), and filtering/enrichment relies heavily on Qwen2.5-VL-72B. The dataset is thus largely distilled from proprietary models, which weakens the paper's thesis that fully open data quality is the bottleneck and raises licensing concerns for redistribution.

Strong backbone confound: Bee-8B is built on Qwen3-8B, a far stronger LLM than the backbones of the fully open baselines it is compared against (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Molmo-7B). The claimed SOTA cannot be attributed to the data curation strategy rather than the backbone; a controlled comparison (same backbone, different data) at full 15M scale is missing.

Evaluation fairness is questionable. The authors use a customized VLMEvalKit with LLM-based judging added to benchmarks like DocVQA/ChartQA/CountBench and patched MathVerse judging, and evaluate Bee-8B in a thinking mode with 16,384-token budgets while it is unclear whether compared models use equivalent settings. Modified judging protocols make the comparison table difficult to interpret and could inflate Bee-8B's scores relative to community-standard numbers.

The full pipeline ablation is only conducted at 1.2M/960K scale, not at the full 15M scale on which the headline results rest, so the claimed pipeline benefits at production scale are not directly evidenced.

Results are selectively highlighted: Bee-8B underperforms semi-open models on several benchmarks (e.g., HallusionBench, MMBench-CN, DocVQA, OCRBench, POPE regresses to 84.0), and the narrative of 'new SOTA' leans on a subset of wins.

Novelty is limited: data curation via rule-based + MLLM-based filtering, LLM-as-judge verification, distillation-based CoT enrichment, and multi-stage training with GRPO are all established techniques; the contribution is primarily engineering and resource release rather than methodological insight.

Key details are under-specified (compute cost, the identity of the proprietary generator models, deduplication/fidelity-verification pass rates, human evaluation of data quality), limiting reproducibility and the ability to assess claims.

strengths: Substantial resource contribution: Honey-Data-15M (15M QA pairs with a dual-level short/long CoT structure) plus the open HoneyPipe/DataStudio curation pipeline represents a meaningful step beyond static dataset releases, and the full-stack release (data, pipeline, recipes, evaluation harness, model weights) supports reproducibility.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Bee-8B is evaluated on ~30 benchmarks across general VQA, document/chart/OCR, and math/reasoning, with comparisons to both fully open (LLaVA-OneVision, Molmo) and semi-open models (Qwen2.5-VL, Keye-VL, InternVL3.5), and consistent competitive results.

Two targeted ablation studies are convincing and well-designed: the D_raw vs D_no-CoT vs D_curated comparison cleanly isolates the effect of noise filtering from CoT enrichment, and the Random-1M vs Honey-Data-1M comparison validates the quality-driven data selection strategy; the appendix further dissects stage-wise and inference-mode (N-T vs T) performance.

The pipeline itself is clearly described with enough detail (rules, verifier prompts in the appendix, dual-level routing logic via fidelity verification) to be reproducible, and the fidelity-verification-failed examples in the appendix give useful qualitative evidence.

Well-organized writing overall, with a clear motivation (data quality over volume for the fully open community) that is coherent and honestly positioned as a data-centric rather than architectural contribution.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core techniques (LLM-based CoT rewriting using existing MLLMs like Qwen2.5-VL-72B and proprietary models, LLM-as-a-judge verification, rule-based filtering, deduplication via perceptual hashing/simhash) are all established; the contribution is primarily an aggregation/engineering effort, and DataStudio itself is barely described despite being billed as a key contribution.

Unaddressed benchmark contamination risk: the training composition (Fig. 3 / Table 7) includes many source datasets (e.g., GeoQA, IconQA, TabMWP, TQA, DVQA, ChartQA, DocVQA-related corpora) that substantially overlap with evaluated benchmarks such as MathVista and ChartQA/DocVQA. No deduplication against evaluation sets or contamination analysis is reported, which weakens the headline SOTA claims, particularly the strong math/reasoning results.

The fidelity verification is circular: enriched responses are verified against the *original* response, so correctness is never independently established; when the original answer is wrong the pipeline either propagates the error (passing the check) or discards valid corrections (the appendix case in Fig. 45 is arguably a correct correction being filtered). No human audit of verification precision/recall is provided.

Ablations are conducted at ~1.2M/960K scale, not the full 15M, so the claimed benefits of the full pipeline at scale are only indirectly supported; ablation results are also shown as figures (Figs. 4-5) rather than precise tables.

Comparison fairness concerns: the paper's customized VLMEvalKit modifications (e.g., adding LLM-based judging to ChartQA/DocVQA/CountBench, patching MathVerse answer extraction) are applied to Bee-8B's own scores, and it is unclear whether baseline numbers come from the same harness; the thinking-mode inference (up to 16K tokens) is also an advantage not consistently available to all baselines.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'establishes a new SOTA for fully open MLLMs' rests on cherry-picked benchmark highlights (several benchmarks show losses, e.g., HallusionBench, OCRBench, DocVQA, AI2D vs Keye-VL), and the paper omits several recent fully open reasoning models from the comparison.

Missing practical details: no compute/cost accounting for the 15M-scale curation and 5-stage training, no license/terms-of-service discussion for redistributing data generated by proprietary MLLMs and for the hundreds of aggregated source datasets, and no statistical significance or multi-seed results.

strengths: Extensive validation: comprehensive ablations (raw vs. filtered vs. CoT-enriched data; curated 1M vs. random 1M), a stage-by-stage checkpoint analysis, evaluation stability across 5 runs, cross-judge sensitivity analysis (Qwen vs. GLM judges), data decontamination analysis, and a blind human evaluation of data quality

Strong empirical results: Bee-8B is competitive with or surpasses semi-open models of similar scale (e.g., InternVL3.5-8B, Keye-VL) across 29 benchmarks, with notable gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks (CharXiv-RQ, MathVerse, LogicVista), supporting the paper's central thesis on data quality
Rare governance rigor for a dataset paper: a full dual-layered licensing framework, per-source license tables, notice-and-takedown policy, and clear attribution of constituent datasets

Commitment to releasing the full stack (corpus, pipeline code, framework, checkpoints, per-stage data, evaluation harness) substantially increases reproducibility and community value beyond a static dataset release
Honest limitations section that explicitly discusses recall/precision trade-offs in LLM-as-judge fidelity verification and the subjectivity of LLM-based evaluation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: LLM-based filtering, LLM-as-judge verification, and CoT distillation/enrichment are now standard techniques (Cambrian-1, MAmmoth-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, etc.); the main contribution is careful aggregation and engineering rather than new methodology

The long CoT enrichment relies on unnamed 'top proprietary MLLMs', undermining both the 'fully open' narrative (the 2.9M long CoT responses are distilled from closed models) and reproducibility; the exact model, prompts, and pass/fail statistics for this stage are not reported

Potential unfairness in model comparisons: Bee-8B is evaluated in thinking mode with 16K-token responses and a customized VLMEvalKit with LLM-based judging on benchmarks where baselines may be scored differently (e.g., DocVQA 87.2 vs. Qwen2.5-VL's 95.5), and the primary judge is from the same model family as Bee-8B's backbone; these protocol choices need clearer justification for head-to-head claims

Attribution is confounded: Bee-8B uses the Qwen3-8B backbone (already a strong reasoning LLM), a five-stage recipe including GRPO, and stage-2 training on 14M pairs—making it hard to isolate how much of the gain comes from Honey-Data-15M vs. the backbone and RL stage; the headline 'SOTA among fully open models' claim partly rests on this confound

Some headline claims are overstated relative to the data: Bee-8B actually trails InternVL3.5-8B on MMMU (66.8 vs. 73.4) and HallusionBench, and 'SOTA' holds only under the specific evaluation protocol

HoneyPipe and DataStudio are described only at a high level in the main text; details needed to reproduce the pipeline (operator configurations, costs, throughput, filter retention rates per stage) are deferred

Human evaluation covers only 38 randomly sampled questions (532 comparisons by 14 evaluators), which is a small basis for validating data quality at 15M scale; the source-level domain labeling based on ~5 manually inspected samples per source is very coarse

Some accounting inconsistencies (e.g., the paper's stated 12.1M short CoT + 2.9M long CoT vs. counts of bypassed OCR samples; unexplained numbers in figures) reduce confidence in the pipeline statistics

strengths: Substantial resource contribution: a 15M-sample dual-level CoT SFT corpus, an open curation pipeline, and an 8B model trained on it, which is genuinely valuable to the fully open MLLM community.

Extensive evaluation hygiene that goes beyond typical resource papers: cross-judge sensitivity analysis (Qwen vs. GLM judge, showing only ~0.3-point global-average shifts), 5-run evaluation stability analysis, data decontamination analysis against all evaluation sets, and inter-model agreement analysis for the verifier (Tab. 7-11).

Well-designed ablations isolating the effects of noise filtering vs. CoT enrichment (D_raw vs. D_no-CoT vs. D_curated) and a Random-1M vs. Honey-Data-1M selection comparison, plus a small blind human evaluation of data quality.
Unusually detailed licensing/governance appendix (Tab. 13-19) with per-source license terms, plus a clear limitations section acknowledging verifier recall trade-offs and LLM-judge subjectivity.
Broad benchmark coverage (29 benchmarks across three task categories) with results broken down by training stage and inference mode (N-T vs. T).
weaknesses: Limited scientific novelty. The core recipe - aggregating existing open datasets, re-captioning/enriching with Qwen2.5-VL-72B, distilling long CoT from proprietary models, LLM-as-a-judge filtering - is well-trodden (MAmmoth-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Molmo, Cambrian-1 all do variants of this). 'DataStudio' and 'HoneyPipe' are presented as headline contributions but are barely technically specified in the paper; no architecture, interfaces, or evidence the framework itself is a contribution beyond the described pipeline.

Evaluation fairness is a real concern. Bee-8B is evaluated with a customized VLMEvalKit (extended LLM judging, 16K-token thinking mode) using a Qwen-family judge, while baseline scores appear to be taken from prior reports under different protocols. The claimed large leads (e.g., +12% on CharXiv-RQ, +5.5% on MathVerse) may partly stem from thinking-mode/LLM-judge settings unavailable to baselines; the GLM-judge sensitivity analysis only re-scores Bee-8B, not the baselines under identical conditions.

Uncontrolled confound: Bee-8B builds on Qwen3-8B, a substantially stronger LLM than the bases of many compared models. The paper attributes gains to data curation but provides no baseline trained with the same backbone on uncurated data at full scale - the 1.2M-sample ablation (Sec. 4.3) is far too small to support the headline claim that 'this significant leap is directly attributable to our data curation strategy.'

Reproducibility caveats understate the pipeline's dependence on proprietary APIs: Stage 4 long CoT is generated by unnamed 'top proprietary MLLMs,' whose identity, cost, and call volume are never disclosed, making the 'reproducible methodology' claim partially hollow.

Decontamination relies on pHash/SimHash, which is weak against paraphrased or reformatted leakage, particularly worrying given the corpus includes MathV360K and related math training sets while MathVision shows the highest overlap counts in Tab. 10.
Human evaluation of data quality is thin: only 38 sampled questions / 532 comparisons by 14 evaluators; no inter-annotator agreement statistics are reported.

Claims are stronger than the evidence in places: 'establishes a new SOTA for fully open MLLMs' rests on cherry-picked wins (e.g., DocVQA 87.0 vs. Qwen2.5-VL-7B's 95.5, and losses on HallusionBench, MMBench-CN, OCRBench, POPE to semi-open baselines are downplayed), and minor numerical inconsistencies between Table 2 and Tables 3-6 (e.g., ChartQA 86.7 vs. 86.1) suggest imprecise reporting.

strengths: The paper delivers a genuinely comprehensive and useful resource suite (Honey-Data-15M corpus, HoneyPipe/DataStudio curation framework, training recipes, evaluation harness, and model checkpoints), which has clear value for the fully-open MLLM community.

The dual-level (short/long) CoT enrichment with a fidelity-verification routing loop is a sensible and scalable data-curation design, and the ablations (D_raw vs. D_no-CoT vs. D_curated; Honey-Data-1M vs. Random-1M) provide direct evidence that both filtering and CoT enrichment contribute measurably, especially on reasoning-heavy benchmarks like MathVista and CharXiv-RQ.

The appendix contains unusually thorough validation for this type of paper: cross-judge sensitivity analysis (Qwen vs. GLM-4.5), 5-run evaluation stability with standard deviations, data decontamination analysis against all 66,682 evaluation samples, inter-model verifier agreement across 32B-235B scales, and a blind human evaluation of data quality (532 pairwise comparisons).

Data governance is handled seriously: a full license/restriction enumeration for every constituent source, attribution tracing, and a notice-and-takedown policy go well beyond community norms for dataset releases.

Bee-8B achieves competitive results against semi-open models (e.g., InternVL3.5-8B) at matched scale, with notable gains on chart reasoning (CharXiv-RQ) and math benchmarks, plausibly supporting the data-quality thesis.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core techniques (MLLM-driven filtering, CoT distillation from stronger teachers such as Qwen2.5-VL-72B and proprietary models, LLM-as-a-judge verification, GRPO polishing) are largely known; the contribution is primarily engineering/infrastructure rather than a new methodological insight.

Comparison fairness is a concern: Bee-8B is evaluated in thinking mode with a 16K-token budget and a customized LLM-judging pipeline (with modified MathVerse judging), while baseline scores are reportedly taken from other configurations; Table 2 does not make clear that all baselines were re-evaluated under identical settings, which inflates the apparent advantage.

The 'new SOTA among fully open models' claim rests on comparisons against only two fully open baselines (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Molmo-7B-D), omitting other relevant fully-open systems (e.g., Cambrian-1, Open-Qwen2VL, Mantis-class models), so the SOTA claim is weakly supported.

Potential residual train/eval contamination risk from aggregating sources that are related to evaluation benchmarks (e.g., ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA sources in training); the pHash/SimHash decontamination is reassuring but hash-based checks can miss paraphrase/derived-content leakage.

The Qwen-family ecosystem dependence is heavy: Qwen3-8B base LLM, SigLIP2 encoder, Qwen2.5-VL-72B for filtering/enrichment, Qwen3-32B judge — it is hard to fully disentangle how much of the gain is attributable to the data curation versus the strong reasoning-capable Qwen3 base LLM, despite the paper's claim that the leap is 'directly attributable' to data curation.

Some design choices are under-justified: coarse source-level domain labels from manually inspecting ~5 samples per source is crude, and the fidelity verification may systematically bias retained data toward outputs consistent with the original (possibly noisy) answers rather than correct ones.
The ablation study is conducted on small 960K/1.2M subsets rather than at the full 15M scale, so the pipeline's impact at the actual training scale is extrapolated rather than directly demonstrated.
